summary: The stroke under your hand is painted in the layer's own pixels by the code that lands it, end taper included, so letting go changes nothing on the canvas: no earlier stroke redraws, goes soft or sharpens, and big brushes no longer slow down as washes pile up.
setup: Photonz Dev, release Next, no flag changed from its default. A 1600 by 1000 canvas (a screenshot's size) or a 4000 by 3000 one for the speed numbers.

try.do: Press B for the Brush, pick Watercolour, and paint three or four washes and two Oil Paint strokes across them.
Zoom to 200% (View, Zoom In until the pill reads 200%) and paint another wash across the earlier strokes.
Let go, and watch the earlier strokes and the end of the new one as the button comes up.
Play the before reel (6x slow motion): at 66 ms after letting go every stroke goes soft, then sharpens.
Play the after reel: held, the moment of letting go, 47 ms on, settled. Nothing moves.
With a mouse, paint a slow Pencil line and watch its end: it thins in as you go, not when you let go.
Paint a dozen large (500 pt) watercolour strokes quickly, one over the next, and feel whether the brush stays as quick as the first.

evaluate: Zoomed in to 200%, does anything already painted change at all when you let go of a stroke?
Does the new stroke look the same the moment before you let go and a second after, end included?
Does the end of a mouse stroke thinning in as you draw feel right, or would you rather it stayed full width until you stop?
With a large watercolour brush over washes that are still wet, does the brush keep up with your hand, or does it still lag?
rough: Reels: 2026-10-27-paint-holds-still-before.mp4 and 2026-10-27-paint-holds-still-after.mp4 (both 6x slow motion, 200% on a 1600 by 1000 canvas, from the walk's frame by frame film). Measured before: at 200% earlier strokes changed in 7 frames after the release (up to 46,481 pixels), 9 strokes were simulated again after one landed, and the held stroke differed from the landed one over 8 to 28% of its reach. After, in painting-holds-still-walk: 0 frames change anything outside the new stroke at 50%, 100% and 200%; one new stroke simulated per scale the layer is shown at; settled 2 to 69 ms after the release.

Not reached yet, so the task stays open: one 120 Hz frame (8.3 ms) at the 95th percentile with a 500 pt brush. Measured on a 12 megapixel canvas with 50 strokes under it, a hand's pace: every medium at 20 pt 2.6 to 7.1 ms; at 500 pt the marker 7.5 ms and a first wash 7.8 ms, but a wash over wet washes 12.7 to 15.8 ms (86 to 112 ms before this work), pencil 13.6, charcoal 16.9, oil 20.6. The 500 pt dry media and oil spend it on their own per-pixel marking, already split across cores, and on drawing the tail again each new dab.

Where the screen resamples the layer (zoomed out, or a 12 megapixel picture at 100% or more), a one-pixel fringe along the new stroke's soft edges and oil's grooves can shift by a few levels as you let go: the live stroke and the picture under it are each filtered on their own before they are laid together. At 100% on a screenshot-sized canvas, where nothing is resampled, the release differs over 0.12% of the stroke. Zoomed 4x on the captures I could not see it.

The probe's film frames (the reels and strips) show faint lines where the live stroke's 256 pixel pieces meet. The real window does not: captures held mid-stroke at 100% on 12 megapixels and at 200% on 1600 by 1000 show no seam (a real one did, and was fixed by hard piece edges).
Zoomed out, the live stroke paints the layer's full pixels rather than the screen's, which is what makes it land unchanged; it costs more pixels a move than before when far zoomed out.

Memory on a 12 megapixel canvas: a kept layer raster is 48 MB, and the shared budget stays 128 MB (the layer before and after the stroke, so undo is instant), let go under memory pressure as before. While a stroke is held its overlay reserves 48 MB but uses only the pages it paints; a smudge copies the layer (48 MB) for the stroke; a stroke's own fields grow with its box (a wash 24 bytes a pixel of it, oil 20).
No mock covers this: nothing on screen moved or changed shape, only when and how the pixels are drawn.
The brush chooser walks still fail to press a brush tile (walks-that-fail-in-the-full-sweep-26 owns them); painting-holds-still-walk picks its brushes with the new pickBrush step instead.
